[quote=-chimor;60141536][spoiler= ¿Who lives who dies?¿ cure or poison?]*[b]Cough cough.[/b]*
Chuki Tampu's cough echoed in the room. Chuskat immediately turned and went to the nobleman, whose arms and legs were tied to the hospital bed, his breathing labored, and he was coughing with fluid coming out of his lungs.
Mochiki approached his superior with a clipboard and immediately asked:
"Sir, of our patients, one has already died (taht was Richimaru) and two are in serious condition (referring to Chuki and Chichimaru). Perhaps... we should..." "
No, I can't imagine abandoning my patients, even if their fate is certain, it seems wrong to me..."
He replied, cutting off his assistant, who insisted:
"Mr. Bracay, these are the director's orders... the medicine and oxygen throughout the country are insufficient for everyone. He tried to prioritize the lives of the youngest."
"So now we're deciding who lives and who dies? Excuse me, I need to go to the bathroom."

Bracay said, leaving, opening the door and looking at himself in the mirror, heavy circles under his eyes and dilated pupils. He placed his trembling hands on the cross on his chest and murmured a prayer to himself. When he finished, he wiped away some sweat from his forehead.
Chichimaru grabbed Mochiki's arm, who was startled by the sudden burning sensation taht gripped him. He turned to her, looking frail, mumbling incomprehensible words. The young man simply lowered his head, his lips trembling, and murmured, "Forgive me."
And then he took one of the nearby medicines, containing a few pills, and took it to another room, where a mitma'ed for llama theft, named Achasisa, worked. She was an assistant to another doctor who cared for six young people with the disease. Mochiki simply stared at her with downcast eyes and handed her the medicines, then said, "Tell them to drink them, to ease the pain and fever."
She handed it back to Mochiki, taking the packet, and thanked him:
"Thank you for your generosity, another assistant."
He said nothing to her, just turned his back and left the room without another word. When he found his superior, distraught at Chichimaru's bed, she was dead. He then asked:
"¿Where were you while she was dying? Mochiki..."
The assistant then sighed deeply and replied:
"I just did... what must be done, the life was no longer salvageable at this point. I delivered the medicine to another room taht was in need..."
[b]On the other side of the country, to the east.[/b]
Ilsainamu, a young man from Rimák who suffered mitma after stealing the sacred coycoy from a temple, had been assigned to serve in the laboratory of Botosí, a qhapac pitipi (imperial city) south of Farfán in Cúma-Apû, the silver mountain. "We're on the one hundred and twenty-seven thousand and four hundred and sixty-sixth simulation... so far, only 100 have shown promise for finding an antiviral, of which 60 have proven toxic, another 35 have failed to combat infected cells, and only 5 may actually be suitable, or have not yet been found to be toxic."
Ilsainamu wrote it down in his reports, then handed it over to the chief scientist, Bawkar, who just sighed:
"We still have a long day ahead of us... but at least we still have one taht work-"
Suddenly, another scientist, Awchar, arrived and informed the chief scientist:
"Sir, CPL B 097, the promising molecule, has proven in recent tests incapable of crossing the blood-brain barrier (brain barrier)."
He saw his superior's dissatisfied expression and immediately suggested:
"But, sir, even so, the failures bring us ever closer to a cure!"
"Hmm, taht makes sense, you two. I want you to keep running simulations. As for the promising ones you find, Ilsainamu found five. Try modifying them by adding fatty acid chains and testing them on infected tissue."
The two nodded at the order:
"¡Yes, sir!"
And then they left the office and returned to the research room.
The next day, Ilsainamu brought another molecule, CPL B 347. It managed to pass the barrier, indeed, apparently a cure, but this molecule, tweaked, ends up attacking healthy neurons through these "tweaks." Upon seeing this, everyone was surprised and horrified by the discovery, and then decided to request support from the laboratories in Chanchán for better resources.
"One hundred and forty-ninth thousand and four hundred and eighth first simulation."
Ilsainamu said, even fewer were detected in this simulation, about 50, of which 25 were discarded, 23 were proven toxic, and only two were ideal. He just sighed and said,
"Two more taht will fail, not the first, nor certainly the last..."
He commented.[/spoiler]

[Spoiler=kûñaches and false promises]
"Life is a river with two tributaries, the herbs taht Camác gave us, and the medicines taht came from beyond the Wichansao Strait, to deny one is to dry up the river, and therefore kill life." The suchu Dokashamu, a suchu from Waskák, a city in Irmasanga, was an elderly man with tanned skin and naturally gray hair taht reached his shoulders, dyed black for appearances. On his forehead was a strip of red cloth with representations of bracay felines (a medium-sized cat with a flat head and a thin body, with fur rich in shades of gray, as well as unique sounds taht sound like "bra bra bra", "brr brr", hence the name) and fish. On his face were light brown eyes under thick eyebrows. His face was taht, but subtle lines below his nose and on his chin suggested taht he shaved his facial hair with some frequency. His clothing included a cape taht went from his shoulders to his waist, with patterns of colorful stripes, blue, red and yellow, along with trees, at his waist, where the cape ended, he had a belt with the representation of a crab, Mûybîkin, the colossal crab taht protected the Wichansao according to mythology, on his legs he wore a traditional chimú skirt with bright colors, and on his feet he wore a common leather sandal, he said this while answering a question from Chán Waname, who, at the command of the sapa, was sent to interview several people, including suchus, to collect information and mainly, from the priests to perhaps know what to do to convince them to trust in modern medicine. Waname was surprised to hear a suchu who was not against science. Dokashamu then explained: "Most suchu, like those who burned medicines in Máchamo for example, or specific willaq umus, do not necessarily hate modern medicine, but see it as a natural adversary of their 'faith' because it is favored over their traditional medicines, but, I tell you and I affirm to you, Mr. Chán, those whose faith is shaken only by something simple like modernity, never had faith, only religion." Chán smiled at Dokashamu's more "open" view, and even gave a friendly handshake: "I am happy to meet such an open-minded suchu, I would like to meet more suchus and willaq umus like you." He said, praising the priest, who then replied: "It's a pleasure, as for the second part, Mr. Chán, suchus like us are only less known because we are less 'noisy', I know you don't see taht, but those who are watching perhaps do, don't create the false idea taht all suchus are radicals who reject modern medicine." "Oh yes yes... I know very well." Chán said turning the microphone to himself, he then thinks: "The Sapa will be relieved to know taht there are suchus and perhaps willaq umus like Dokashamu out there too." Meanwhile, in another neighborhood of Waskák, a little less privileged, a little girl of maybe 7 years old walked through the dirt streets of her neighborhood, she wore simple cotton clothes on top and a patched skirt taht reached her knees, on her wrist she wore a bracelet of fibers, and on her feet she walked in simple sandals, her skin was dark and eyes were very dark brown, her black hair was braided in a somewhat sloppy, but subtle way, it was Cámana, the same one taht the empress hid medicines between masks, in her hands she carried a simple, handmade basket, with Kûñaches (chimú cheese breads) inside, she offered them to people passing by on the street, few really even looked at her while she offered, and even fewer were interested in buying... It was like taht, after hours on the street without success taht she saw Dokashamu, the suchu walking calmly through the streets, they were emptier than usual, so anyone who If he walked around there, he would attract some attention. When he saw the little girl, he looked at her with pity, feeling sorry for her situation, and then approached. She then offered him one, already somewhat reluctantly: "one kûñache, ¿please? It's for my sick mother..." Dokashamu then took out from under his cloak, in a pocket in the robes he wore underneath, a wallet, and took out a single Chayhuac coin, worth 300 Chayhuacs. The coin was made of copper and nickel, on the edges it was already common the presence of silver. It shone with a whitish tone. In the center was the number 300, below was the drawing of mountains and above the value was a drawing of the moon. And on the back, perhaps the most interesting, the smiling cat, a Bracay with closed and relaxed eyes, with a calming smile. Although it has sharp hurries, they do not seem threatening. The details in the drawing are meticulous, made precisely with the intention of not being counterfeited. Above it was written, both In both traditional and Latin writing, the name of the current emperor, Chumun Caur. When he handed over the coin, the little girl was immediately surprised and hugged the suchu. She clung to his leg, tears streaming down her face. As she stammered her thanks, he simply placed his hand on her head and said, "Well, well, little girl... I'll buy them  all so you can go take care of your mom,¿ ok?"
He smiled as he took the kûñaches and placed them in his robes, between his cape and robes below. She thanked him again, and then left. When he arrived, it was close to sunset. Upon entering, the smell there was of pumpkin and alcohol. He again saw his mother still on the sofa. Her olive skin looked pale, and her dark eyes looked exhausted, her hands calloused, and her clothes were of worn cotton. She looked with dark circles under her eyes at her own daughter. When she sat down, she sat with some difficulty and put on the mask made by the "kind woman." Seeing the empty basket and her daughter showing the only coin, she smiled. She wanted to show her smile, she wanted to hug her, but she knew she couldn't. So she just put a glove on her side and put her hand on her head. When she touched her mother's hand, Cámana felt taht she was a little less hot, but her mother didn't talk so much anymore to see if the medicine was really working... The next day, when she got up from her old bed of her mother, feeling small on the large mattress and covered by the well-detailed blankets, as she left the cotton pillow behind, Cámana went to the main room, where her mother was sitting, looking at the tube television, the smell now was not of pumpkin, which they already ate every week, now it was Llárâma (sweet potato) and pápá (potatoes), both common foods in coastal areas, her mother simply greeted: Good morning daughter. Cámana smiled when she heard her mothers voice, and responded with another: Good morning. She looked at the table where the potatoes were, the steam escaping through the window suggested they were still warm, as she picked up and chewed one of the potatoes, feeling it melt in her mouth with a buttery and soft flavor, she took another one, with her small hands did the same, she would leave the rest for her mother, and then sat down next to her, she then pointed to her daughter to watch the television: There, a suchu, Dokashamu, seemed to be offering coins to children in need, alongside others, an act of charity, whose only price was to hear their stories, her mother said nothing, but Cámana understood, she should go there, she was happy to know taht today money would be easier than other days. Arriving there, she saw the same suchu who had given her the 300 chayhuac coin. He smiled when he saw her. He gave her a slightly smaller coin, 100 chayhuac, this time with a beautiful flower on it. The old man then began to tell a story as 12 children, including Cámana, sat down: "Añchay añchay nanban (Hello, children! Have you heard of the...¿medicine taht cures all diseases?" They shook their heads. Cámana seemed particularly curious to hear. Dokashamu then took out a container with a kind of cream inside. He said: "This is achicamác, Cámac oil, made from the toxins of a frog mixed with the bark of the Páwàri tree, along with the nectar of tóchaì, it is capable of curing...everything! Even wounds, my friend, Opaywamu, will show you!" He comes to the side and sees Opaywamu putting a simple lipstick on his wrist to symbolize blood. He asks, "Sir, ¿is this ethical?" He replies, in an equally low tone, "I will explain later. Now, give me your arm." Opaywamu then extends it to Dokashamu, who quickly places it on his fingertips and applies it to Opaywamu's "wound." It is, of course, removed. While the children watch in amazement, another suchu distributes them. The children look in amazement at the "miracle." He smiles as they watch, and then explains, "Ah, but of course, in this case, it's somewhat useless to use. After all, Achicamác only works well when someone is very, very ill! And in this case, it's not even the real one." Cámana, however, was so focused on the medicine and the miracle taht she doesn't seem to have noticed or cared about the last part, which the other children, though older, seem to already know is a hoax. He cleared his throat and then continued, "Now,¿ shall we hear your origin story? Don't think I came here just to tell you about a 'miracle' cream!" He smiles as he sees the children nodding yes, he then begins to tell: "A long time ago... when Wápìwan would have taken Bechup Pañan and take them to Táncûy (boatman of the dead) to guide them down the river to the Wápítî (kingdom of the dead), Camác confronted him as he took a life, and worst of all, without him being able to face him, then Wápìwan, with his wisdom suggested, 'then,¿why don't you give them what protects against disease? I am not an executioner, I just do my job, just as where there is light, there is darkness, where there is life, there is death', and it was like this, taht Camác no longer created just fruits or vegetables for humanity, he also began to create medicinal herbs, along the sea, Muyvery and Cochanamo who decided to also help with algae taht would serve as medicine, for those who did not want their souls taken by Wápìwan, Camác created the achicamána, over 4 millennia of history, from kurakas to emperors have sought such medicine, many have died poisoned...perhaps its existence is not even real, but in the end, of course, always prefer modern medicine, if not, herbs, after all, this isn't even achicamác, as I said, no one has figured out how it's made, I'm only here to act as hope maker for all of you, little ones...wait a minute, ¿where's the other girl?" Dokashamu said confused when he saw taht Cámana was no longer there, she must have left a little after the myth began, he felt a twinge of pain, imagining her using the cream on her mother and seeing taht it wouldn't work "She must not have heard taht the cream isn't real." Dokashamu thought already feeling guilty, however, he saw taht she didn't go very far, he said pointing to Opaywamu: "Now, Opaywamu will explain to you how it would be made, and why no one has ever replicated it." He then stood up, while Opaywamu took his place, Dokashamu then followed Cámana home, he saw her through the window, his mother weakened, and Cámana telling her about the story, his mother listened attentively, while taking the coin taht her daughter handed over, she however, did not use the cream, as he left towards the table, Dokashamu crouched down, standing against the adobe wall, and heard the little girl saying: "taht man said it only works when someone is very, very ill... maybe I should take a break and see if Mommy doesn't get better before..." Dokashamu, said nothing, he covered his own mouth with his hand, while holding back a muffled cry, while tears ran down his cheek like rivers, he wanted to apologize, but now would not be a good time, he knew taht, he would wait until he saw her again and explained the truth to her, yes it was a good plan... in his head at least.
[/Spoiler]
